title: aiSure™ — More AI Opportunity. Less AI Risk. (Munich Re, Insure AI)

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts that AI deployment brings uncertain performance, legal exposure and potentially significant operational losses, and materially extends the cluster by proposing insurance-backed warranties and coverage as a complementary risk-transfer mechanism. It does not, however, address task selection, verification or workflow redesign, and its product claims are not independent evidence of effectiveness.

st.t: AI insurance: Coverage cannot replace professional governance
st.an: Munich Re supports the cluster’s narrower claim that insurance transfers specified AI performance risks rather than providing comprehensive protection. It distinguishes warranty-backed vendor liabilities from coverage for deployer losses and offers deployment examples, but provides no claims-performance evidence and does not suggest that coverage displaces governance or legal duties.

kp.k: Uncertain returns can inhibit AI investment
kp.d: The page reports that 98% of CEOs anticipate immediate business benefits from implementing AI, while 60% hesitate to invest because of uncertain returns. The supplied document provides no survey attribution, sample size, methodology or fieldwork dates for these figures.

kp.k: Performance warranties transfer risk to AI vendors
kp.d: Munich Re describes a mechanism in which an AI accuracy warranty reduces buyers’ perceived purchase risk but creates a contractual liability for the vendor. It presents insurance-backed warranties as enabling providers to indemnify clients for financial losses or legal liabilities directly related to AI errors; this is a description of the offering, not evidence of achieved investment returns.
qs: Providing a **performance warranty** for the AI model's accuracy de-risks the purchase decision, but it creates a liability on the balance sheet of the tech company.
aiSure™-backed performance warranties enable you to indemnify your clients for their financial losses or legal liabilities directly related to AI errors.

kp.k: AI errors create operational losses and legal exposures
kp.d: The source identifies contractual liabilities, corporations’ own financial losses and legal liabilities as distinct consequences of AI performance errors. It lists discrimination, IP infringement, hallucinations and regulatory fines among exposures for vendors and adopters, and additionally identifies privacy leakage and harmful generated content. Its coverage descriptions are broad and tailored, rather than detailed policy terms establishing that every listed exposure is covered in every case.

We welcome other coverage requests and are happy to explore designing a bespoke solution for your business.

kp.k: AI insurance targets recurring performance errors
kp.d: Munich Re characterizes AI insurance as a category it pioneered in 2018, triggered by unexpected errors during ordinary model use rather than only catastrophic losses or third-party damages claims. It argues that frequent, individually small errors can accumulate into substantial economic losses or class-action exposures that existing insurance does not address. These are the insurer’s category and coverage-gap claims.
qs: AI insurance is a new category of business risk coverage.

Unlike traditional casualty policies protecting against catastrophic loss or traditional liability covering third party damages claims, AI insurance, pioneered by Munich Re in 2018, is triggered by unexpected errors in the ongoing performance of AI models in daily business use.

This makes it suited to covering high frequency, low severity events which in the aggregate can create significant economic loss or class action exposures that existing forms of insurance simply don't address.

kp.k: Technical safeguards cannot eliminate underperformance risk
kp.d: The FAQ argues that AI is both probabilistic and systematic, so mistakes may persist until identified and corrected. It says technical means cannot fully avoid underperformance, while failure to use AI effectively may create competitive disadvantage. Insurance is consequently framed as a financial backstop against excessive losses, not as a method for correcting model errors.
qs: AI is probabilistic – it makes the decisions based on the probability of a range of outcomes.
AI is systematic – meaning it will continue to make these mistakes until they are identified and corrected.
The risk of underperformance cannot be fully avoided by technical means.
By indemnifying AI vendors and their corporate users against excessive losses, aiSure™ fills a risk management gap, protecting AI innovations with insurance.

kp.k: Partnerships distinguish performance failures from cyber attacks
kp.d: The page reports that Mosaic Insurance and Munich Re offer AI performance-failure coverage using a parametric-like structure intended to deliver fast, objective claims for vendors and deployers. It also reports an iTOO partnership bringing aiSure to South Africa, distinguishing non-malicious performance failures from traditional cyber threats. No claims-processing measurements or payout results are supplied.
qs: Mosaic Insurance has partnered with Munich Re to harness the power of aiSure™ — a visionary product offering that covers AI performance failures using a parametric-like structure for fast, objective claims aimed towards AI vendors and deployers.
AI introduces a new layer of risk beyond traditional cyber threats, with performance failures that aren't caused by malicious attacks.
iTOO and Munich Re have partnered to bring aiSure to South Africa.

kp.k: Lending example covers prediction errors and model drift
kp.d: The MKIII example describes an AI loan decision model for credit unions backed by insurance covering losses from prediction errors, calibration or data drift, unexpected deviations and changes in borrower behavior. This is a named application of performance-risk transfer, not a quantified finding about lending expansion, accuracy or reduced losses.
qs: MKIII — AI-powered loan decision model for credit unions.
MKIII’s model is backed by Munich Re’s aiSure™ insurance, covering losses from prediction errors, calibration or data drift, unexpected deviations, or shifts in borrower behavior.

kp.k: Valuation warranties allocate error costs through insurance
kp.d: The Barkr example describes a concrete allocation of liability in AI-powered alternative-asset valuation: Barkr warranties its valuations and pays the difference if they are wrong, while Munich Re indemnifies Barkr under the warranty. The page presents this as supporting lender confidence but supplies no measured effects on lending decisions or profitability.
qs: Barkr also warranties its values, paying the difference if they’re wrong.
This provides additional security, as Munich Re covers Barkr's warranty.
By indemnifying Barkr for its liabilities under the warranty it gives lenders and banks confidence in their decisions.

kp.d: The page lists predictive cybersecurity, earthquake early warning and fraud prevention as applications with performance guarantees, alongside warranty-backed crop plans. It separately describes Instnt’s fraud-loss insurance program as supported by Munich Re reinsurance capacity. These examples document the source’s claimed breadth of applications, without providing comparative performance studies, policy limits or loss histories.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Munich Re claims that AI creates business opportunities alongside performance-related financial and legal exposures, and that specialised insurance can transfer these risks and support adoption.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain insurance source, not a claim about changes to legal practice. Munich Re states that AI adoption promises immediate benefits but uncertain ROI inhibits investment. It claims that AI errors can cause poor decisions, interruption, lost revenue and accumulated liabilities, including discrimination and IP infringement. It describes underperformance as a risk that technical measures cannot fully eliminate and says ineffective AI adoption can create competitive disadvantage. Its proposed response is insurance covering vendor performance warranties, corporate losses and legal liabilities arising from AI errors. Munich Re presents performance warranties as a way to reassure purchasers while creating contractual exposure for vendors. It also claims that specialised AI insurance addresses recurring performance errors that existing insurance does not adequately address. Named applications include lending, valuations, fraud prevention, cybersecurity, earthquake warning and agricultural adoption; their performance benefits are presented as commercial claims rather than legal-sector findings.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source offers CEO sentiment figures, Munich Re’s experience since 2018 and named commercial deployments, but no supporting study methods or quantified insurance outcomes.
pts.d: Munich Re reports that 98% of CEOs anticipate immediate AI benefits and 60% hesitate because of uncertain ROI; the supplied document does not identify the survey, sample, fieldwork dates or methodology. It supports the availability and proposed mechanisms of risk transfer with named partnerships: Mosaic’s parametric-like performance-failure cover, iTOO’s South African offering, insurance backing for MKIII’s loan decision model, reinsurance capacity for Instnt and indemnification of Barkr’s valuation warranties. Other named applications illustrate claimed operational benefits and performance guarantees. These are provider-reported examples, not independent evaluations. No claims-payment data, comparative adoption results, measured ROI improvements, accuracy benchmarks or quantified loss reductions are supplied. Munich Re also invokes its experience in AI insurance since 2018.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The claims concern current commercial offerings and ongoing daily AI use, with a claimed category origin in 2018 rather than a dated forecast of future transformation.
pts.d: The document is labelled 2026 and describes existing offerings and partnerships. Immediate business benefits are attributed to CEO expectations, not demonstrated implementation results. Munich Re says performance insurance is triggered by unexpected errors during ongoing business use and is suited to frequent, individually modest events that can aggregate into substantial losses or class-action exposures. Vendor indemnification is tied to losses or liabilities directly related to AI errors, while corporate cover is discussed in the context of deployment at scale. Specific covered risks vary by application: MKIII’s example includes prediction errors, calibration or data drift and shifts in borrower behaviour. The source describes tailored or bespoke insurance, but provides no policy wording, exclusions, limits, premiums or precise payout thresholds; its broad risk list should therefore not be read as an unconditional promise that every listed risk is covered in every policy.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are AI vendors, corporate deployers, insurers and business customers, with downstream effects on borrowers, farmers and people exposed to AI errors.
pts.d: Vendors face warranty obligations and AI-related liabilities but are offered insurance as a means of reassuring prospective clients. Corporate adopters face operational losses, legal damages, reputational harm and customer attrition, with insurance presented as a financial backstop. Insurers and reinsurers are presented as developing a new business-risk category, including through Mosaic and iTOO partnerships. Sector examples identify credit unions and borrowers, lenders using luxury assets as collateral, businesses managing fraud and cybersecurity, online sellers, agricultural retailers and farmers, and facilities benefiting from earthquake warnings. The source also identifies potential harms to people through discriminatory outputs, privacy leakage and harmful generated content. It does not identify law firms, lawyers or legal-service clients as a distinct affected market.
